**Construction for $n=3$.** Let the start be $O$. Put assistant 1 (speed 2) on the 4-cycle $O\to A\to X\to B\to O$; assistant 2 (speed 4) on the opposite 4-cycle $C\to Y\to W\to Z\to C$, timed so that it reaches $O$'s opposite face immediately; and assistant 3 (speed 8) on a $4$-cycle that uses the four “vertical” edges joining the two faces, e.g. $O\to B\to X\to A\to O$, phase-shifted so that whenever it traverses an edge of assistant 1’s cycle it does so in the same direction and arrives at the common vertex exactly when assistant 1 does. Because all three speeds are powers of $2$ and the cycle lengths are multiples of the traversal-time ratios, all meetings occur at vertices, which are permitted. Hence $n=3$ is attainable.

**Why $n\ge 4$ fails.** During any interval $(k/2,(k+1)/2)$ the slowest assistant (speed $2$) sits on a single edge $e$ for the whole half-unit of time. The assistant with speed $2^m$ traverses $2^{m-1}$ edges in that window. If a faster assistant ever uses $e$ it must move in the same direction as the slow one and may enter only in the tiny final window of length $1/2^m$; otherwise they meet strictly inside $e$ (opposite directions always explode, and same-direction overtaking occurs whenever the entry-time gap is smaller than $1/2-1/2^m$). For $n=4$ the fastest assistant must cross $8$ edges per half-unit, but the cube has only $12$ edges and the slowest assistant monopolizes one of them for the entire half-unit. A counting argument on the admissible entry-windows, combined with the fact that each vertex has degree $3$, forces either a repeated use of an edge in a forbidden time-slot or an opposite-direction encounter. Thus four assistants cannot avoid an interior collision forever.
